Conditions and time limits:
- The complaint must be in writing and made by the payee or the holder in due course [2].

Yes, a cheque bounce case can be settled by compounding the offence. Every offence punishable under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is compoundable, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as stated in Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
negotiable instrument presumption as to consideration holder in due course
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 rebuttal of presumption consideration
rows.answer:
It shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration, according to Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1].

In K.P.O. Moideen Kutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr. [1996] 2 S.C.R. 227, the Supreme Court noted that Section 118(a) is a presumption of law that throws the burden of proof of failure of consideration on the maker of the promissory note [11]. The initial burden rests on the plaintiff to prove execution, upon which Section 118 imposes a duty on the court to raise the presumption that the instrument was made for consideration, shifting the burden of establishing that the promissory note is not supported by consideration to the defendant [11].

rows.answer:
- An agreement becomes a contract if it is made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and is not expressly declared to be void, according to Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].
- In the Supreme Court judgment of "U. P. Rajya Nirman Nigam Ltd. versus Indure Pvt. rows.question: What is free consent in contract law?
queries: What is free consent in contract law?
free consent coercion undue influence fraud misrepresentation mistake contract voidable

consent caused by coercion undue influence fraud mistake void agreement section 19
rows.answer:
Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake [1][12]. Consent is considered so caused when it would not have been given but for the existence of such coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 13 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which covers how two or more persons are said to consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense [5].
- Section 14 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which defines free consent as consent not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake [1].
- Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which provides that when consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused [2].
- Section 19A of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which provides that when consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused [4].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?

rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to an agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, making it a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

However, a contract is not voidable if consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, as stated in the Exception to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Furthermore, a fraud or misrepresentation that did not cause the consent of the party on whom it was practised or to whom it was made does not render a contract voidable under the Explanation to Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

rows.question: What counts as fraud that makes a contract voidable?

rows.answer:
Fraud that makes a contract voidable includes any of the following acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party thereto or his agent, or to induce him to enter into the contract, as provided under Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872: [1]
- the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true [1].
- the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact [1].
- a promise made without any intention of performing it [1].
- any other act fitted to deceive [1].
- any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent [1].
Mere silence as to facts likely to affect willingness to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances of the case are such that it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech, under Section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualification
Indian Contract Act section 11 capacity of parties to contract
Indian Contract Act section 12 sound mind for purpose of contracting
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1
rows.answer: Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12]. A person is considered to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time of making it, they are capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon their interests, according to Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [2][12].

rows.question: Can a court award reasonable compensation when a contract fixes a penalty for breach?
queries: Can a court award reasonable compensation when a contract fixes a penalty for breach?

rows.answer:
Yes, a court can award reasonable compensation when a contract fixes a penalty for breach, and the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the penalty stipulated for, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused [1][11]. This is supported by the Supreme Court judgment in "B.S.N.L versus RELIANCE COMMUNICATION LTD.", which notes that under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a contract is breached and a penalty is stipulated, the party complaining is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the penalty stipulated for [1]. Furthermore, the Supreme Court judgment in "M/S. KAILASH NATH ASSOCIATES versus DELHI DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY & ANR." explains that in cases where the amount fixed is in the nature of penalty, only reasonable compensation can be awarded not exceeding the penalty so stated, with the penalty serving as the upper limit beyond which the court cannot grant reasonable compensation [13].

rows.question: How far is a surety liable for the debt of the principal debtor?
queries: How far is a surety liable for the debt of the principal debtor?

Indian Contract Act section 128

rows.answer:
The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract, as stated in Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. As explained in the Supreme Court judgment "Bank of Bihar Ltd. versus Damodar Prasad & Anr.", under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, save as provided in the contract, the surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, making the surety liable to pay the entire amount with immediate liability that is not deferred until the creditor exhausts remedies against the principal debtor [1]. For instance, where a bill of exchange is guaranteed and dishonoured by the acceptor, the surety is liable not only for the amount of the bill, but also for any interest and charges which may have become due on it, according to Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, according to Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [1][5]. Furthermore, when a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [5]. Additionally, under Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, whoever being under sentence of imprisonment for life commits murder shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life [9].

Dowry death is defined as where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage, and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry [1][3]. In such cases, the husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death, as stated in Section 304B of the Indian Penal Code, 1845 [1] and Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [3].

The punishment for committing dowry death is imprisonment for a term of not less than seven years, which may extend to imprisonment for life, under Section 304B of the Indian Penal Code, 1845 [1] and Section 80 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [3].

A person accused or suspected of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail by an officer in charge of a police station, a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, a High Court, or a Court of Session, subject to specific statutory restrictions and exceptions [1][2][3][9]. 

However, such a person shall not be released on bail if there appear reasonable grounds for believing they have been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life [1][3][9]. Furthermore, they shall not be released if the offence is a cognizable offence and they were previously convicted of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for seven years or more, or previously convicted on two or more occasions of a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years [1][3][9].

rows.question: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty in a sale of goods?
queries: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty in a sale of goods?

topSources: The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 s12

rows.answer:
A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of a contract of sale, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated, while a warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated, under Section 12 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 [1]. This distinction is also discussed in the Supreme Court judgment Rajratan Babulal Agarwal versus Solartex India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors [11].
